newsitem.title: KENYA: Congo airlift of Rwandan refugees passes 40,000.
newsitem.headline: Congo airlift of Rwandan refugees passes 40,000.

text.p: A U.N. airlift of Rwandan Hutu refugees from former Zaire passed the 40,000 mark on Wednesday but aid officials say thousands more remain scattered across the country.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR, told Reuters more than 1,000 refugees were flown to Rwanda's capital Kigali from Kisangani and Mbandaka in the new Democratic Republic of Congo.
More than 40,000 refugees have been repatriated since the airlift began in earnest in April 27.
Kessler added that thousands more Rwandan refugees were gathering at Mbandaka in the hope of joining the airlift.
"There are about 10,000 refugees there and more are arriving every day," he said. "We are also still getting 30 to 40 refugees a day emerging south of Kisangani."
Kessler, speaking from the northern town of Kisangani, said UNHCR officials had on Tuesday been allowed to travel farther than 48 km (30 miles) south of Kisangani for the first time in weeks.
But they had gone little further before turning back after seeing the wreck of a vehicle which recently hit a landmine. He said aid officials were seeking a military escort before going further.

Biaro and Kasese, makeshift sites for nearly 85,000 Hutu refugees, emptied on April 21 after attacks by local villagers and then rebel soldiers before the start of the U.N. airlift to take them back to Rwanda.
More than 35,000 drifted back and have since been flown home, but aid officials have no idea where the rest might be and Congo and Rwandan officials deny such large numbers exist.
Fears for the refugees increased following evidence of massacres earlier this month by rebel soldiers at Mbandaka, 500 km (300 miles) to the west of Kisangani.

Witnesses told Reuters rebel soldiers killed over 300 unarmed refugees at Mbandaka days before Kinshasa fell to the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL) lead by Laurent Kabila, who declared himself president.
Residents in Kisangani have also told of hundreds, possibly thousands of those who fled Biaro being butchered and their bodies burned at a point 52 km (32 miles) south of the city.
Kabila has strongly denied his forces had any role in massacres and has said those who commit atrocities would be punished.
More than 1.5 million Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 to escape reprisal for the genocide of up to 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Most returned when Kabila's forces began their offensive at the end of last year, but more than 300,000 others -- including a hard core of former Rwandan Hutu soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen and their familes -- fled farther west.

Nearly 3,000 refugees remain at Ubilo, 80 km (50 miles) south of Kisangani, and officials report the number rising by around 50-60 a day. UNHCR is sending a train to Ubilo on Thursday to collect 1,200 of them.
